column8: Thu 19 Nov: 3e and Table 3's yields row: Throsby's artist works her day job only up to her survival line, so the plan buys Treasuries only up to the ten's need (IPS l.11's order, l.13) and a cheaper ten sends more to the floor and to shares (Q171-002, dated); the contrast that lands with a finance judge is a pension glide path (Q7-025, Q115-030), where a rise in funded status moves money into bonds, never 'a judge expects'; breaks named: artists obey loosely (rows 3-4) and the response runs only on the three trade days; Throsby read as Rengers and Menger state him, his chapter abstract only; one outside name per part.

Thu 19 Nov: register evidence for Q171-001, every figure in NUMBERS 4 'On a later curve' and 5(e): on the 13 Nov curve no top-up, $6,203 left over, VT $31,544, $105,000-$125,000; fix: never call the $75,001 the top-up (WORDS: the top-up is the $2,388 alone; say the payments take half the deposit); the 13 Nov figures dated, a note never a re-size; the 1.30-point case in prose only as a distance, about 1.3 points, no odds (NUMBERS 5, What the report says); twin figures in Q98-014 are the parallel stand-in, these are the exact ones.

Thu 19 Nov: store: the day-job response is real for creators but small (+2.6 hours a week of art when the outside wage doubles) and established artists work fewer hours for better money; evidence for Q171-001's break, never a figure in prose.

Thu 19 Nov: store: Q171-001's break (no rise in arts hours among part-time musicians); abstract only, and the sample is Uruguayan on RePEc, Peruvian in Hartog and Kackovic (card Gaps); never cited without the full text.
Thu 19 Nov: store: the work-preference model fits creative artists better than performers (Korea, abstract only); supports Q171-001's frame for a writer, never evidence about Laura herself.

Thu 19 Nov: 3a, one clause if any: a 2026 study paid 2,400 New York artists $1,000 a month and found 3.9 more hours a week on art and 2.4 fewer on other work, so a residency passes certainty to residents only if its own money is certain (IPS l.11); fix: never 'Caplet's closing line measured' or 'proved' (a matched comparison, only part randomised, first-survey response 55.8% paid against 23.3% control); the trial chose on need, a residency on merit; absorbs Q171-007; one outside name per part.

Thu 19 Nov: the same trial's second result (arts earnings flat, 'more personally meaningful' is the authors' reading); carry it in Q171-006 if used; as a 3d guard only, never promise co-sponsors residents' earnings.

Thu 19 Nov: store or closing colour: Menger's uncertainty as a lure sits beside IPS l.19's division (risk on the page, none in the promises) but maps no decision and names no break; OCR'd JSTOR copy, check the wording before quoting.
Thu 19 Nov: Rosen alone was refused as a duplicate (H3-117) and Q1b-012 holds scale and cyclicality; it earns a place only as half of the pair in Q171-011.

Thu 19 Nov: the cost disease is in the store (Q102-027 to -031, H3-112); this adds only the contrast with scalable work, carried by the pair; check pp. 162-164 in a library copy (read in a 1978 reprint on pdfcoffee).

Thu 19 Nov: 2.3's lead: she earns where one book's work reaches any number of buyers and will spend where a stay takes the same hours as ever, so the payments are bought from money already earned and the 2028 deposit carries only what can wait (IPS l.9, l.13); fix: not 'all ten from the 2027 deposit' (on 6 Nov the ten cost $302,287 and the 2028 deposit completes them, NUMBERS 1); Taiwan's 4.92% fall is average earnings with bonuses and weakens the claim, so keep only the minimum wage held at NT$17,280 through 2008-2010, or no Taiwan figure; two names break panel 4's one-name rule in 2.3, so name Baumol and say Rosen's point plainly; -7.8% stays the Census figure (Q148-005); absorbs rows 9, 10 and 13 (its break: she is unscalable in making, so the plan hedges the market for her art, not the art).

Thu 19 Nov: Q136-029 holds the 73.9% as 2.3's one figure (about three-quarters smaller, at today's rates) and Q134-039 the plan relying on her career once; 'Rosen money' is a label only, though 'the deposit most at risk is asked for least' can join that row's wording.
Thu 19 Nov: Q171-011's break column; Q12b-016 holds the graphic novel's years; the line that the plan hedges the market for her art, not the art, goes with Q171-011.

Thu 19 Nov: Q158-011 (arts revenue moves with GDP, 0.51) and H9-013 hold procyclical arts money on newer data; Baumol and Bowen's Depression low adds history only, and it is performing arts, not books.

Thu 19 Nov: 2.3 or 3a: her three incomes are Menger's kindred activities, diversified against one book failing and not against a recession, the finance reader's split of specific and market risk, so the portfolio must hold what a recession does not hurt (IPS l.9's counterbalance); break: 2020 split them (Q56-012), and a Treasury for each date pays in either kind; one outside name per part; OCR gaps.

Thu 19 Nov: 2.3, beside Q171-015 or not at all: artists usually spread risk through second jobs, and Laura is the rare one able to use financial assets, so the portfolio is her hedge (pitch l.3), not a second job; Menger's 'unusual' describes the labour route, never 'artists do not invest'; one Menger clause per part.

Thu 19 Nov: 2.0 or 2.3, one clause: the pitch's stock she can't sell is also one she can't insure (Menger: only some occupational risks in the arts are insurable; France's authors are outside even its artists' unemployment scheme), so the only insurance she can build is a portfolio that does not fall with her career; fix: the case never says where she lives or is insured, so say authors seldom can, never as her own law; French authors may use the self-employed allowance if they qualify; Senat read as an excerpt; the human-capital frame is Q1-024's and Q134's; absorbs Q171-018.
Thu 19 Nov: the US case of the same point (Pandemic Unemployment Assistance, 2020-2021); one episode, and the case does not say where she is insured.

Thu 19 Nov: 3a source for Q171-021: Baumol and Bowen's actors 'as real a financial contribution as the gift of any patron' is the line that makes the artist the last donor; 1960s Broadway, not a residency; check the page in a library copy before citing.

Thu 19 Nov: store: Abbing's theses 60-61 (artists' own unpaid work relieves the cost disease; stars aggravate it); 'Laura, a star, can pay in' is Keel's reading; Dutch visual artists; behind Q171-019 if used, one name per part.

Thu 19 Nov: 3a's why for IPS l.11's one step further: in the arts the last donor is the artist (Q171-019), so a market fall that reached the payments would land on residents as fewer places, shorter stays or smaller stipends (Q102-031); fix: never 'no resident ever pays for a market fall', since a fall before the 2031 move lowers the stated top and the building it pays for (NUMBERS 8p): say no year's operating money depends on a share price; residents are the likeliest place, not the only one; beside SD-3 (first money in a field of last money), never two last-money lines in one part.

Thu 19 Nov: Q37-021, H4-048 and Q10-013 hold dollars certain, not what they buy (about 70% at 2.4% for 2042, NUMBERS 8d, checks); the new clause, that the gap falls on residents unless co-sponsors, grants or fees fill it (case l.85-86), goes there for 3e and 3d; the case's limit (l.90), not the plan's.
Thu 19 Nov: 3d wording guard only: a residency buys time and work for a few and never lifts artists' incomes (Abbing, Dutch state subsidies); store.

Thu 19 Nov: store: a residency will not lack applicants (Abbing thesis 38, Menger on oversupply); fix: money is not its only uncertain input (building costs, staff pay and the Taiwan dollar are uncertain too, Q102, NUMBERS 8q), so drop that clause.
Thu 19 Nov: the same Smith chapter; a prize-winner paying back the blanks is colour, and Abbing (Q171-023) says paying the blanks draws more players in.

Thu 19 Nov: 2.3's opening or 3.0, one clause if Smith wins the part's one name: IPS l.9's 'You'd think' is Smith's 1776 finding that the temper which picks a lottery profession leaves its house uninsured (nineteen in twenty), and the plan insures the promises and gives the taste for risk only money promised to no one (l.15); break: Laura has drawn a prize and her risk is thoughtful; Smith earns the place on chapter I.10's content, never as an echo of Caplet's own Wealth of Nations joke (19 Nov: not a request); absorbs Q171-025.

Thu 19 Nov: 3d or one conceit turn in 3a: an open promise to keep an arts house going (Vanbrugh's 20,000-pound opera fund, 1720) always needed more, while ten fixed dated sums can be owned in full before the doors open; the fixity is the case's (l.90), the plan's choice is to buy it in January 2027; Vanbrugh and the Academy not checked at source (Baumol and Bowen give the surname only), p. 161 in a library copy before citing; one turn per part, never in tables or Laura's words; absorbs Q171-028.

Thu 19 Nov: same page as Q171-027; 3d's line that her share is fixed in dollars and cost growth above it is the co-sponsors' to plan for is Q37-021's and case l.85-86's; 'no respite' is the source's quote only.
Thu 19 Nov: store: the residency's design is outside the plan (case l.164); abstract only.

Thu 19 Nov: 3c, one clause: in 1960 New South Wales wrote into law that the Opera House's estimate 'shall not, under any circumstances, be exceeded by more than ten per centum', and it cost about 9.5 times that limit (nominal; $102m excludes organ and car park; Keel arithmetic checks); Laura's figure holds because it counts Treasuries she owns, not a cost (IPS l.15), and case l.114's worry is promising more than she can give; break: a dearer building moves onto co-sponsors and her flexibility; absorbs Q172-002, -008 and -030; never 'cannot move' or 'cannot overrun' for a stated figure (NUMBERS 3); one Opera House fact per part, and Q155-015's Pencil Booking is 3d's.
Thu 19 Nov: Q172-001's figure: the cap's last form ($85m) and four amendments read; each amendment's figure UNVERIFIED; never '$102m broke the $85m cap' (scope differs).

Thu 19 Nov: 3c, the order reversed: the Act let the Treasurer advance money against lottery tickets not yet sold (s 4), so the building ran ahead of its money, while Laura's figure is owned first, then stated (IPS l.15); a founder has no Treasurer behind her; absorbs Q172-032 (say it plainly; ink stays owned Treasuries, never lottery cash).

Thu 19 Nov: 3b source for Q172-019: 496 lotteries and 86.7 million tickets raised $102m from 1957 to 1986, 13 years past the opening, a flow that chased the overrun, while Laura's portfolio has two deposits; H7-086 holds 'lottery-paid', this adds the counts and the 13 years; how much of the post-1973 money repaid advances was not read.
Thu 19 Nov: $7m to $102m and 'lottery-paid' are H7-086's; Cahill's early start is the commit-then-find-out order Q172-003 states with the Act's own words.
Thu 19 Nov: Utzon's 'costs should be a secondary consideration' (reported speech, source not listed) is the designer's view when no budget binds, the foil for Q172-027; one Opera House fact per part.
Thu 19 Nov: the card's own verdict: a picture only, nothing beyond H7-086's fixed dollars, never a share of the building's cost.
Thu 19 Nov: a re-estimate halfway ($35m, five times the first) is still an estimate of a cost; Q172-001 carries the contrast; undated.

Thu 19 Nov: store: whoever controls payments controls the project (1965), but the change of control did not lower the cost, so as a reason for the half kept it cuts both ways; the 80% is a magazine's figure.
Thu 19 Nov: store: a fee tied to cost rewards overruns; outside the report's job (case l.164).
Thu 19 Nov: store: an overrun's cost falls on the name on it (Flyvbjerg interview); architects are not donors; never in 3f.

Thu 19 Nov: store or a 3b clause: 'great buildings overran' is a survivors' story (Flyvbjerg on Hirschman's sampling), and the cultural houses that closed for money are Q9-016's; never imply the Opera House was in Hirschman's sample.

Thu 19 Nov: 3c source for Q172-014: Sawyer's line, as Hirschman quotes it, that the project would not have been begun had its cost been known; the 1967 article read as an excerpt; development projects, not a residency.

Thu 19 Nov: 3c aha candidate: the plan takes Hirschman's side for the building and the other side for her money: ignorance of cost may start the residency (case l.164: its total cost 'has not been determined') because a design can be redrawn to a budget, while every figure Laura names is owned because no creativity makes a Treasury pay more than it says (IPS l.15); break: Flyvbjerg finds the rescue in about one project in five (Q172-015, -016), so the building cannot count on it either, which is her flexibility's work; Hirschman's mechanism quoted through his critic; never 'exact' for a stated figure (NUMBERS 3); one outside name per part.

Thu 19 Nov: 3b or 3e: Flyvbjerg's test of 2,062 projects (costs 1.39 times estimate, benefits 0.90; the malevolent hand in 80%, the rescue in about one in five) carries Q172-014's break; mostly transport and energy, real terms.

Thu 19 Nov: 3b evidence that a building's use does not rise to pay for its overrun (24 buildings: costs 1.36, benefits 0.99); fix: never beside Q9-025's +62% for buildings without naming the samples (24 large public buildings in one table against the 2023 book's base rates), and the small-building class is Q5d's; one sentence with Q172-015 in prose.
Thu 19 Nov: store: no learning in a century (overrun -0.5% a year, benefits worse); the larger samples do not support a trend, so never 'estimates will not improve' as a finding.

Thu 19 Nov: 3b clause candidate: Willie Brown's dig-a-hole line names the pull of a half-dug building on whoever cannot walk away, in a small residency often the founder; fix: her flexibility 'promised to no one' keeps it hers in words and never stops her choosing to pour it in (card idea 2(c)), so never 'no hole is dug on her account'; the column itself not read (two secondary quotes).

Thu 19 Nov: 3b aha candidate: the three famous overruns here were paid by payers whose money kept coming (lotteries to 1986, a parliament, a city's taxpayers), and Laura's portfolio gets two deposits, the last in January 2028, so she states only what she owns and keeps half the shares promised to no one (IPS l.15); fix: never 'her money stops' (the case lists 'continued business income' among sources for the rest of the facility, l.85-86; it is the portfolio's deposits that stop); say 'the three', not 'every famous overrun', and name what kept coming or it reads as a tautology; break: the residency's other payers may be deep (Q103-037).

Thu 19 Nov: store, or one clause beside Q172-022: Holyrood's 90 million pounds to 431 million (4.8 times, Keel arithmetic checks); a parliament's landmark; Q172-001 carries the cost-against-money contrast.

Thu 19 Nov: SC-4 (Q150-015) holds that a building's first figure leaves out what becomes the overrun; Holyrood's omitted contingency, fees, fit-out and VAT is one more example; never imply her 0.5% margin covers building fees.

Thu 19 Nov: 3b, one clause: Audit Scotland's 'whatever construction method is adopted the client always pays for risk' says why the founder's side, not the funders', needs the flexibility IPS l.15 names first for building costs that overrun (with SC-4: funders cap grants); her flexibility plus anything above the top covers a rise of about 25% if shares earn the 7.5% assumed (NUMBERS 8u, checks); break: Holyrood's client could keep paying, Laura's portfolio cannot (Q172-019).
Thu 19 Nov: settle cost against time and quality before design; Q172-028 carries what an owned figure does for the design; the residency's priorities are not the team's to set (case l.164).

Thu 19 Nov: Kahneman's curriculum team is the outside view's own story (Q13-009 to -011 hold it); 'take the decision out of the room' is precommitment, held by Q7-030 and card Q137; a time overrun, not money.

Thu 19 Nov: 3c, pedigree, one clause: 'think slow, act fast' closes the window in which things go wrong; the move before the 2031 meetings closes Laura's window by owning, not by speed, so say owned before it is named, never that the plan acts fast; what stays exposed (building prices, the Taiwan dollar, others' pledges) is IPS l.15's three uses; absorbs Q172-026.
Thu 19 Nov: the Empire State Building and the Opera House's 14 years illustrate Q172-025; CONFLICTING (16 from the 1957 competition), so 14 only with 'from the start of work in 1959'.

Thu 19 Nov: 3d candidate: target costing fixes the cost first and designs to it, so an owned figure named in 2031 is money the residency's design can be fitted to two years ahead; fix: never 'a figure that cannot fall' (NUMBERS 3: an early fund end at zero interest can leave the top short), never the 15% as a saving to expect (the developers' own action research on chosen projects, abstract only); say what the figure allows, never advice on the design (case l.164); absorbs Q172-006.

Thu 19 Nov: 3d: SD-1's 'her figure is their target' carried from the funders to the architect: her owned figure is the part of the building's budget already in hand; fix: never 'cannot move' (NUMBERS 3); the case asks for no construction budget (l.164); absorbs Q172-023.

Thu 19 Nov: Q5d-005 places a fifth at about P60 and a quarter at about P70-75 from an approved budget, and NUMBERS 8u the about 25% cover; the new clause, that a Holyrood is met by the building changing (size, funders, timetable) and never by her promise, goes there; never 'sized' or 'contingency fund'; say 20% to 25%, since WORDS keeps 'about a quarter' for the first $39,162.
Thu 19 Nov: the same contrast as Q172-001 (an estimate of a cost against a count of money held), with case l.114 carried there; never 'cannot overrun' for a stated figure (NUMBERS 3).

Thu 19 Nov: Table 3 candidate only if its one page has room: watch the building's timetable (design, tender, start), since her flexibility waits on a window the plan cannot date; a watch, never a third reason to change (IPS l.17).
Thu 19 Nov: the conceit worker's note is Q172-003's fact said plainly; ink is owned Treasuries, never lottery cash; one Opera House fact per part, and Q155-015 already holds one.
